title: English Vocabulary 2 · Units 15–16
description: Reviewed vocabulary and constructions related to romantic relationships, weddings, separation, daily routines, meals, personal care, housework and leisure.

units.title: Unit 15 — Romance, marriage and divorce
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 15. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe stages of a romantic relationship using date, go out with, break up, get to know, and be in love.
Distinguish getting engaged, getting married, a wedding, a marriage, and a wedding reception.
Use natural marriage-related grammar, especially get married to someone and marry someone.
Describe pregnancy, birth, anniversaries and celebrations using accurate word families.
Explain relationship breakdown using go wrong, give up, leave someone, on your own, and get divorced.

items.example: They arranged a date for Saturday evening.
items.note: A planned romantic meeting; not a calendar date in this sense.

items.example: Their first date was at a little café.
items.note: The first planned romantic meeting with someone.

items.example: She has been going out with Alex for six months.
items.note: In this unit, have a romantic relationship with someone; different from go out socially.

items.example: They broke up after two years together.
items.note: End a romantic relationship; past tense: broke up.

items.example: He broke up with his girlfriend last month.
items.note: The preposition with introduces the person whose relationship ended.

items.example: This is her first serious relationship.
items.note: A relationship that matters greatly to the people involved.

items.example: Their relationship changed after university.
items.note: Here it refers to a romantic relationship; it can also refer to other personal connections.

items.example: I got to know him during our first semester.
items.note: Describes becoming familiar with a person over time; do not use know for the process.

items.example: We are just friends, not a couple.
items.note: The relationship is not romantic.

items.example: They realised they were in love.
items.note: Describes a strong romantic feeling.

items.example: I think she is in love with her colleague.
items.note: Use with before the person.

items.example: They got engaged during their trip.
items.note: Become formally committed to marrying each other.

items.example: They have been engaged since March.
items.note: An adjective describing someone who has agreed to marry.

items.example: They announced their engagement yesterday.
items.note: The noun related to engaged; the formal agreement to marry.

items.pt: um par de; cerca de dois
items.example: We spent a couple of days by the coast.
items.note: Usually means two and sometimes a few; followed by a plural countable noun.

items.example: The young couple have just moved into a new flat.
items.note: Two people in a romantic relationship; also used of two things or people.

items.example: Their romance began during a summer course.
items.note: A romantic relationship or the feeling of romantic love.

items.example: They are getting married next spring.
items.note: Use get married, not get marry or get marrying.

items.example: Paula got married to Sam last year.
items.note: Use married to someone, not married with someone.

items.example: My grandparents have been married for fifty years.
items.note: Be married describes marital status; get married describes the change.

items.example: She married her partner in June.
items.note: Marry someone has a direct object: marry Alex, not marry with Alex.

items.example: Their marriage has lasted thirty years.
items.note: The state or relationship of being married; do not confuse it with the wedding event.

items.example: The ceremony will start at noon.
items.note: A formal event held to mark an important occasion.

items.example: They planned a small wedding by the sea.
items.note: The event when two people get married; marriage is the relationship or state.

items.example: The wedding ceremony lasted half an hour.
items.note: The formal part of the wedding.

items.example: The reception was held in a nearby hotel.
items.note: Here a party or gathering after a wedding, not a hotel reception desk.

items.example: They invited sixty guests to the wedding reception.
items.note: A party after the wedding ceremony.

items.example: The newlyweds went to Portugal for their honeymoon.
items.note: A holiday taken just after getting married.

items.pt: ir para a lua de mel
items.example: They went on a honeymoon after the wedding.
items.note: Use on with a honeymoon.

items.example: The bride arrived a few minutes early.
items.note: The woman on her wedding day.

items.example: The bridegroom stood beside the bride.
items.note: The man on his wedding day; groom is a shorter form.

items.example: The groom thanked the guests.
items.note: Short for bridegroom in a wedding context.

items.example: Her husband works at the hospital.
items.note: A married man in relation to his spouse.

items.example: His wife joined us for dinner.
items.note: A married woman in relation to her spouse; plural: wives.

items.example: She got pregnant the following year.
items.note: Become pregnant.

items.example: She is pregnant with her second child.
items.note: An adjective: expecting a baby.

items.example: She had a healthy pregnancy.
items.note: The noun related to pregnant.

items.example: Their first daughter was born in April.
items.note: Use be born, not be borned.

items.example: Their first child was born last year.
items.note: Child is singular; children is plural.

items.example: Today is the anniversary of their first meeting.
items.note: The same date one or more years after an important event.

items.example: They celebrated their tenth wedding anniversary.
items.note: The date on which a couple got married, remembered each year.

items.example: There was a celebration after the good news.
items.note: A special event or activity to mark a happy occasion.

items.example: We celebrated her graduation at home.
items.note: The verb related to celebration.

items.example: They had a small celebration with close friends.
items.note: Have a celebration is a natural verb–noun combination.

items.example: The divorce was difficult for both of them.
items.note: Can be a noun or a verb; in this example it is a noun.

items.example: They got divorced two years ago.
items.note: A marriage officially ends; compare get married.

items.pt: dar errado; começar a dar errado
items.example: Things went wrong after they moved.
items.note: Become problematic; past tense: went wrong.

items.example: He was alone in the house.
items.note: Without other people.

items.example: She was on her own all weekend.
items.note: Alone or without other people; change the possessive for the person.

items.example: He did not want to give up his job.
items.note: Stop doing an activity or trying; separable when it takes a noun object.

items.example: She decided to leave her partner.
items.note: Here end a romantic relationship or stop living together; not simply depart from a place.

items.pt: mudar-se para fora de uma casa
items.example: He moved out after the separation.
items.note: Leave a home to live elsewhere.

items.example: After the separation, he lived on his own.
items.note: Possessive variant of on your own.

items.example: They agreed to get a divorce.
items.note: A noun-pattern alternative to get divorced.

units.title: Unit 16 — Daily routines
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 16. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Differentiate wake up, get up, go to bed, go to sleep, and fall asleep.
Describe meals and eating habits using have breakfast, have a snack, main meal, takeaway, and feed.
Describe personal hygiene using have a shower, have a bath, brush your teeth, and put on make-up.
Use natural housework collocations: do the washing, do the ironing, do the shopping, and make the bed.
Contrast go shopping with do the shopping and eat out with eat in.
Discuss leisure routines using spare time, weekdays, stay in, go out, come round, and once a week.

items.example: I usually wake up at seven.
items.note: Stop sleeping; you may still be in bed.

items.example: Please wake me up before eight.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb: wake me up, not wake up me.

items.example: I get up ten minutes after I wake up.
items.note: Get out of bed; different from wake up.

items.example: We usually go to bed by eleven.
items.note: Going to bed does not necessarily mean immediately falling asleep.

items.example: He went to sleep within a few minutes.
items.note: Start sleeping.

items.example: She fell asleep while reading.
items.note: Start sleeping; similar to go to sleep.

items.example: I replied to her message straight away.
items.note: Immediately, without delay.

items.example: I had a late night because of the party.
items.note: Stay awake and go to bed late; compare have an early night.

items.example: I will have an early night before my exam.
items.note: Go to bed earlier than usual.

items.pt: tirar um cochilo; dormir um pouco
items.example: I had a short sleep after lunch.
items.note: A short period of sleep, often during the day.

items.example: During the week, she works in the city.
items.note: On weekdays rather than the weekend.

items.pt: à noite; no período da noite
items.example: I usually read in the evening.
items.note: Use in the evening, not at evening.

items.example: She has cereal and fruit for breakfast.
items.note: Breakfast food made from grains; often eaten with milk.

items.example: We usually have breakfast at eight.
items.note: The usual expression for eating the morning meal.

items.example: I had a light lunch before the meeting.
items.note: Eat a small midday meal.

items.example: A salad makes a light lunch.
items.note: A meal that is not large or heavy.

items.example: I had a snack after the lesson.
items.note: A small amount of food between meals.

items.example: We had a snack before the film.
items.note: Have + noun expression for eating something small.

items.example: Our main meal is usually in the evening.
items.note: The largest or most important meal of the day.

items.example: She did not bother to cook that evening.
items.note: In this sense, make the effort to do something.

items.pt: não se dar ao trabalho de
items.example: He did not bother to make breakfast.
items.note: The verb is followed by to + infinitive in this pattern.

items.pt: não se dar ao trabalho de fazer algo
items.example: I do not bother with a cooked lunch.
items.note: Use with before a noun phrase.

items.pt: comida para viagem; pedido para comer em casa
items.example: We ordered a takeaway instead of cooking.
items.note: British English: food from a restaurant eaten elsewhere; American English: takeout.

items.example: Let’s get a takeaway tonight.
items.note: Buy a prepared restaurant meal to eat at home.

items.example: Remember to feed the cat this evening.
items.note: Give food to a person or animal; past tense: fed.

items.example: I feed the cat before going to bed.
items.note: A common verb–noun combination.

items.example: We had coffee after breakfast.
items.note: Have is often used for food and drink.

items.example: I have a shower after the gym.
items.note: British English: have a shower; take a shower is also possible.

items.pt: lavar-se; dar uma lavada no corpo
items.example: I had a quick wash before leaving.
items.note: Wash yourself, often without having a full bath or shower.

items.example: Remember to clean your teeth before bed.
items.note: British English phrase meaning brush your teeth.

items.example: The children brush their teeth after breakfast.
items.note: An alternative to clean your teeth.

items.example: She put on make-up before the party.
items.note: Apply cosmetics; make-up is normally an uncountable noun.

items.example: She carries a little make-up in her bag.
items.note: Cosmetics used on the face. Usually uncountable.

items.example: She used a bit of make-up for the photograph.
items.note: A small amount of something, often uncountable.

items.example: I sometimes have a bath after a long day.
items.note: Different from have a shower.

items.example: We walked instead of taking a taxi.
items.note: Followed by a noun or -ing form; not instead of to take.

items.example: He likes to lie in the bath and listen to music.
items.note: Lie here means rest horizontally; past tense lay.

items.example: My father has a shave every morning.
items.note: Shave is also a verb: he shaves every day.

items.example: He shaves before work.
items.note: The verb for removing hair with a razor.

items.example: They share the housework fairly.
items.note: Work done to keep a home clean and tidy; uncountable.

items.example: We do the housework on Saturdays.
items.note: Use do with housework, not make.

items.example: Fortunately, nobody was hurt.
items.note: Means that something good happened because of luck.

items.example: Luckily, the bus arrived on time.
items.note: Similar to fortunately; often introduces a positive outcome.

items.example: A cleaner comes to the office twice a week.
items.note: A person whose job is to clean homes or other buildings.

items.pt: lavar roupa; fazer a lavagem de roupas
items.example: I do the washing on Sunday morning.
items.note: Here washing means cleaning clothes, not washing yourself.

items.pt: lavagem de roupas; roupas para lavar
items.example: The washing is drying in the garden.
items.note: In a housework context, clothes being washed or already washed.

items.example: She does the ironing while listening to a podcast.
items.note: Ironing means making clothes smooth with an iron.

items.pt: roupas para passar; ato de passar roupa
items.example: There is a pile of ironing in the bedroom.
items.note: The household task of pressing clothes with a hot iron.

items.example: He makes the bed every morning.
items.note: Use make the bed, not do the bed.

items.example: I do the shopping on Thursday evenings.
items.note: Usually refers to buying food and household supplies.

items.example: They went shopping for clothes at the weekend.
items.note: Often refers to shopping as a leisure activity; contrasts with do the shopping.

items.example: She learns to play the guitar in her spare time.
items.note: Time when you are not working or doing required tasks.

items.example: The library is open every weekday.
items.note: Any day from Monday to Friday.

items.example: I usually study on weekdays.
items.note: Plural of weekday.

items.example: We decided to stay in and watch a film.
items.note: Stay at home, especially instead of going out.

items.pt: sair de casa; sair para se divertir
items.example: They often go out on Friday evenings.
items.note: In this unit, leave home for leisure; different from go out with someone romantically.

items.example: We eat out once a week.
items.note: Eat at a restaurant rather than at home.

items.example: We saved money by eating in.
items.note: Eat at home instead of at a restaurant.

items.example: The team meets once a week.
items.note: Frequency phrase: once a week, twice a month, three times a year.

items.pt: vir visitar; aparecer na casa de alguém
items.example: A few friends came round for dinner.
items.note: British English: visit someone at their home, often informally.

items.example: They chatted about their plans.
items.note: An informal conversation or the verb for having one.

items.example: We chatted about our holidays.
items.note: Use about to introduce a subject of conversation.

items.example: I usually visit my family at the weekend.
items.note: A common British English time phrase.

items.example: We ordered a takeaway because nobody wanted to cook.
items.note: A natural expression for arranging delivery or collection of prepared food.

items.example: I usually get home before six.
items.note: Use get home without the preposition to.

items.example: She replied straight away when I called.
items.note: Combines the verb reply with the time adverbial straight away.
